The QoQ jump came from clearly higher turnkey cloud shipments plus more NRE projects reaching the tape-out stage (mask and test-wafer billings are large in amount but lower-margin, versus Q1's early-stage NRE which carried a higher gross margin). quarterly_data.signal: Pre-payments rose notably in Q2 because GUC pre-buys materials for large CSP turnkey programs - besides CoWoS it must secure HBM stacks and substrate ahead of the build so everything (substrate, HBM, the SoC from TSMC) arrives together for packaging. GUC sells the customer the finished CoWoS package with HBM inside; if HBM prices rise the chip price rises with it, so the cost risk sits with the customer, not GUC. Management cited HBM pricing going from about 240 at the start of the year to 700 and up to 900 (as spoken; unit not stated), fully passed through. Whether HBM procurement flows through GUC's own P&L or is booked as a service fee is still being worked out case by case at this early stage.

quarterly_data.signal: Optimus supply chain has to be built or in-sourced: 'with Optimus, there is no supply chain. Optimus power electronics and circuit boards are all Tesla-designed but fabricated by suppliers today; OPTIMUS 4, to be built in Austin, will be much more vertically integrated (PCB work brought in-house), with an aspirational 10 MILLION UNITS A YEAR versus 1 MILLION UNITS A YEAR for Optimus 3. quarterly_data.signal: Power as the binding constraint on AI compute (Musk): 'we think power constraints are going to be a major issue for AI, just turning on the AI computers... even the hyperscalers are having trouble turning on their AI compute and finding the power and then smoothing the power - especially for the training runs where the power cycles dramatically in a very short period of time. He added the US has ~1.2-1.3 terawatts of power production against ~0.5 terawatt average usage, so batteries could potentially double US energy output.

quarterly_data.signal: CALL-ONLY: THE JUNE-QUARTER SHORTFALL WAS A LEADING-EDGE NODE SHORTAGE, AND IT GETS WORSE IN SEPTEMBER. Cook: June-quarter supply constraints hit 'primarily the Mac, and to a lesser extent, iPhone and iPad', and 'the constraints were primarily driven by the availability of the ADVANCED NODES that our SoCs are produced on'. Root cause is 'not a regular supply issue - it's a DEMAND FORECAST issue' (iPhone +22% and Mac +29% ran ahead of Apple's own high expectations). 'We are seeing LESS FLEXIBILITY in the supply chain than normal... we've been pulling supply ahead. At some point, there's a limit to that.' For the September quarter the supply-constraint impact 'increases SIGNIFICANTLY sequentially' and now spans iPhone, Mac AND iPad - 'we've got a quarter that we're going to be scrambling on the supply side'. Asked whether adding a second US fab operator would help, Cook rejected the premise: 'this isn't a partner or supplier issue.'
quarterly_data.figure: Sept-qtr constraint impact up SIGNIFICANTLY QoQ; iPhone + Mac + iPad all constrained

quarterly_data.signal: CALL-ONLY: '100-YEAR FLOOD' ON MEMORY PRICING - APPLE RAISED PRODUCT PRICES BECAUSE OF IT. Cook: 'we reluctantly raised prices... we did it because we're in what I would characterize as a 100-YEAR FLOOD on the memory pricing, with EXPONENTIAL INCREASES in memory prices' (prices already raised on iPad and Mac; elasticity 'too early' to judge, channel inventory delays the read). Cost path: Dec < Mar < Jun ('significantly more' than March, partly offset by carry-in inventory) < Sep ('we expect to pay EVEN HIGHER memory costs'), with the carry-in-inventory offset DECREASING beyond September; 'if you look beyond September, we see the market pricing for memory CONTINUING TO INCREASE, which could drive an increasing impact on our business'. Structural read from the largest non-datacenter DRAM buyer: 'primarily the DRAM market has THREE SUPPLIERS. Obviously if there were more suppliers, that would be good, and it would help us on the supply side and perhaps the pricing side... We're EVALUATING ALL OPTIONS.'
quarterly_data.figure: Memory prices rising exponentially; Sep memory cost higher again; DRAM = 3 suppliers

quarterly_data.signal: CALL-ONLY: MEMORY IS NOW THE ENTIRE MARGIN STORY, QUANTIFIED. CFO Parekh's bridge: total-company GM 49.3% (Mar qtr) -> 48.1% (Jun qtr, ex-tariff-refund) = -120bps, and 'MORE THAN 100% of that can be explained by the MEMORY COST change' - FX 'was a factor' but 'the main driver was really the memory cost impact'. The same holds into the September guide: 48.1% -> 46.5% midpoint (ex-refund) = -160bps, again more than fully explained by memory, with partial offsets from carry-in inventory, lower non-memory component costs and favorable mix. Reported June-quarter GM was 50.1% INCLUDING ~2pts of tariff refunds (products GM 40.1%, +140bps QoQ including >2.5pts of refunds; services GM 75.6%, -110bps on mix). September guide: revenue +9-11% YoY (FX -2.5pts sequential + rising supply constraints), iPhone mid-teens, GM 47-48% incl. ~1pt refunds, opex $19.1-19.4B, tax ~16.5%.
quarterly_data.figure: Jun GM 48.1% ex-refund (-120bps, >100% memory-driven); Sep guide GM 47-48%, rev +9-11%

quarterly_data.quarter: Onto Innovation Citi’s Global TMT Conference 2026 (09-09-2026)
quarterly_data.signal: A new growth leg is forming in power semiconductors from data center power. Onto's earlier power-semi run was driven not by capacity expansion but by customers using Onto's inspection and metrology to drive yield improvement, with yields in the 60%-70% range rather than the 90s. The EV recovery has not really happened yet, but those same customers are now telling Onto they see demand from data centers driving adoption of power semiconductors and that Onto needs to prepare. Management is not seeing the actual orders yet and has no good clarity on timing, but said 2027 into 2028 is what the customers are thinking about; because the process control is already inserted in their process, Onto should benefit as they expand. Data center power is relatively small for Onto today and would be captured under specialty devices.

quarterly_data.quarter: Onto Innovation Citi’s Global TMT Conference 2026 (09-09-2026)
quarterly_data.signal: CFO Brian Roberts on the margin path and supply: 2026 margin gains have come from operational productivity and the move of manufacturing from the U.S. to the international extended factories - a year ago Onto was shipping its first tools from those factories and in Q2 it shipped about 70% of its tools from them. To date Onto has driven 250 basis points of gross margin and doubled that at the operating margin line. Into 2027, the accretive Dragonfly G5 and Atlas G6 add ASP lift which, alongside productivity, drives toward 'a margin that starts with a six'. The two major 2026 headwinds were memory cost and freight/fuel shortage, partly offset by being in region, and Onto is having pricing conversations with customers about the existing product portfolio for the 2027 pricing/budgeting season. On supply, the extended-factory move gave Onto partner capacity and new clean rooms without heavy CapEx; the supply chain is not perfect but Onto is using customer visibility to get ahead of bottlenecks, is carrying a higher inventory balance, is not missing customer dates and its lead times have not grown too much.

quarterly_data.signal: First cost and gating condition put on the EUV plan the Q3 call described only as partnerships: 'we have a plan to go to EUV, but a full EUV program would cost us about $300 million. For a company generating $850 million to $900 million in annual revenue, you're very cautious about doing that... you could end up crippling the company if you're not careful.' The approach is to introduce certain EUV capabilities in stages over what Moreau called 'probably takes us a good maybe a five-year investment cycle', spreading the cost while waiting for the captives to release EUV work to merchant suppliers. The demand gate today is thin: 'At the moment, there's one company out there that's requesting EUV masks. That's not a big enough market for you to incur that $300 million.' EUV is critical from 14 nanometers down to 3 nanometers and essentially all of that mask business is captive today.
quarterly_data.figure: full EUV program would cost about $300 million against $850 million to $900 million of annual revenue; one company currently requesting EUV masks; EUV critical from 14 nanometers down to 3 nanometers

quarterly_data.signal: Mask-set ASP ladder and share, quantified: citing a Morgan Stanley Japan initiation report on a competitor, Moreau said a 90 nanometer design is about 25 masks per set and roughly '$50,000 of revenue for that one chip design'; at 14 nanometers the set goes to close to 80 masks and 'we're talking about $1 million in revenue contribution'; at five nanometers 'you're talking about $10 million to $20 million for that one semiconductor chip design, for the photomask set' - 'a very parabolic move'. Photronics holds about 10% of the total photomask market including captives, captives are about two-thirds of the market and gained share in 2025 purely on ASP (conceivably going to 70%), while display share is about 28% and has held steady for five years. On units, Photronics estimates it manufactures about as much volume as TSMC does in-house, but that TSMC's fully captive mask output would be worth 'at least five or six times' Photronics' roughly $620 million of semiconductor photomask revenue last year if it carried an external price.
quarterly_data.figure: 90 nanometer set about 25 masks and about $50,000; 14 nanometer set close to 80 masks and about $1 million; five nanometer set $10 million to $20 million; Photronics 10% of the total photomask market, captives about two-thirds going possibly to 70%; display share about 28%; semiconductor photomask revenue about $620 million last year

quarterly_data.signal: Node-capability roadmap by site, more granular than the Q3 call. Boise is the U.S. high-end facility and 'can produce masks down to seven nanometers' today, with little revenue at 7 nanometers so far, and 'with the same equipment, we are advancing our capabilities to actually go down to four' - not ready and no revenue presented today. Allen, Texas is being taken from 180 nanometers and 130 nanometers up to 65 nanometers and 'we should be up and running in the next month or two'; production then shifts out of Boise to Texas, freeing Boise to capture more 7, 10, 14 and 22 nanometer business. Korea is the other upgrade: the bulk of that facility's business today is about 40 nanometers, the expansion to 8 nanometers is expected 'in about a year from now', and Photronics expects significantly greater 8 and 10 nanometer business there 'largely because of customers that are very close to that facility'. The U.S. is 17%-19% of revenue today and is expected to be a higher share of total revenue in fiscal 2027.
quarterly_data.figure: Boise down to seven nanometers today, advancing toward four; Allen, Texas from 180 and 130 nanometers to 65 nanometers up and running in the next month or two, freeing Boise for 7, 10, 14 and 22 nanometers; Korea about 40 nanometers today to 8 nanometers in about a year; U.S. 17%, 18%, 19% of revenue rising in fiscal 2027

quarterly_data.signal: Mechanism behind the better-than-expected July quarter, which the Q3 call did not spell out. April-quarter push-outs came from customers being unable to capture memory and from Asian fabs at unusually high utilization telling chip designs 'You have to delay your design because we don't have the capacity for it'. Through the July quarter those designs started to be released because the same fabs 'added capacity in the 14-nanometer, 22-nanometer, 28-nanometer range', and in some cases told a customer with a 40 nanometer design 'if you move that chip design to 28 nanometers or 22 nanometers, I will then manufacture it for you' - i.e. the capacity shortage is actively forcing node migration, which is the ASP-positive trend Photronics benefits from. On the display side Korea is strong on high-end consumer electronics launching this fall while China has pulled back because low-end consumer electronics cannot capture memory; Moreau relayed that the memory companies are talking about 'another 2, 3, 4 years before supply and demand comes into equilibrium'.
quarterly_data.figure: fabs added capacity in the 14-nanometer, 22-nanometer, 28-nanometer range and pushed 40 nanometer designs to 28 or 22 nanometers; memory supply and demand equilibrium another 2, 3, 4 years away

quarterly_data.signal: Capex cycle and the financing constraint behind it. Photronics historically spends about 10% of revenue on capex; the upgrade cycle that began last fiscal year continues this year and 'then it likely extends into next year', and Moreau would imagine fiscal 2028 'probably remains elevated above the traditional 15% of total revenue range'. The balance sheet has $673 million of cash, but $504 million of it sits in the two 50/50 semiconductor joint ventures (Taiwan, entered 2013-2014; China, 2018-2019; ownership 50.01%) and can only be spent at those facilities - dividending $100 million out returns roughly $40 million after the partner split and a 20% tax, 'not a really productive use of cash'. Only about $165 million of cash sits outside the joint ventures, so 'if we need cash, we would either issue debt or a line of credit... Not likely to use equity'. Next-quarter guidance was 'basically flat to slightly up sequentially' with gross margin, most recently 33%, 'about flattish' in the coming quarter; the full-year capex guidance was cut on equipment delivery delays but the revenue timelines for both the Texas and Korea expansions were maintained.
quarterly_data.figure: capex historically about 10% of revenue, likely elevated above the traditional 15% of revenue range in fiscal 2028; $673 million cash of which $504 million sits in the two 50/50 joint ventures and only about $165 million outside; gross margin 33% and about flattish next quarter

quarterly_data.signal: Named the biggest headwind of the last couple of years as geopolitics rather than demand: Photronics lost China-market customers it had good business with after 'We were told by the U.S. government, You have to stop shipping to that customer', and in another case Taiwan put a customer on its restricted list, forcing Photronics to move that production out of its Taiwan facility into its China facility, which has less capacity - so revenue with that customer fell as well. Offsetting structural positive: regionalization and reshoring, with TSMC expanding very aggressively in Arizona and GlobalFoundries and Samsung also expanding in the U.S.; the more locations that manufacture chips, the more mask business spreads out, which is why Photronics is expanding in the U.S. and Korea.
